title: Purchasing
subtitle: Suppliers, requisitions, purchase orders and goods receipts
summary: Purchasing converts real business needs into controlled supplier orders and verified stock receipts. The journey starts when Inventory detects low stock, continues through a requisition and an approved purchase order, and ends when accepted goods enter Inventory. Finance then needs to account for goods received and amounts owed to suppliers. This is the first half of the Procure-to-Pay story: from demand to receipt, before Accounts Payable settles the supplier invoice.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Segregation of duties is built in: the buyer who raised an order cannot approve it (PROCUREMENT_SEPARATE_APPROVER). Only ACTIVE suppliers can receive orders.

Posting a goods receipt calls Inventory's receipts API to add the stock, then posts GOODS_RECEIVED: debit inventory, credit 2110 goods received not invoiced (GRNI). AP later clears GRNI when the invoice arrives.
If Inventory is down, posting fails cleanly with a message and can be repeated without double booking.

sections.title: Purchasing explained in plain English
paragraphs: Imagine the stable manager sees that oats are running low. Rather than ordering casually from a supplier, the club creates a purchase requisition: an internal request describing what is needed. A buyer turns the approved requirement into a purchase order (PO): the formal order sent to the supplier.

When the truck arrives, the receiving team records a goods receipt against that PO. Each receipt line says which PO line was delivered, where the goods are going and how many units were accepted. Inventory Control—not Purchasing—owns the stock balance.

The purchasing process creates evidence. It answers who requested, who approved, what was ordered, what arrived, how much was accepted, and where it went. That evidence later supports Accounts Payable matching and financial audit.

sections.title: Why purchasing matters to Finance · the GRNI bridge
paragraphs: Buying and receiving are not the same as paying. A purchase order expresses the club’s intention to buy. A goods receipt proves goods arrived and were accepted. An AP invoice records the supplier’s claim for payment. These are different records and often arrive at different times.

GRNI stands for Goods Received Not Invoiced. Suppose 55 units are accepted at a hypothetical unit cost of $10: the accepted inventory value is $550. Under an illustrative perpetual-inventory accounting rule, receipt can debit Inventory $550 and credit GRNI $550. When AP posts the matching invoice, the GRNI liability is cleared or reclassified according to the actual configured posting rules. Payment follows in AP/Treasury.

This separation helps prevent a company from paying for goods it never received, accepting the same delivery twice, or overstating stock and profit. The three-way match compares purchase order, goods receipt and supplier invoice; it is an AP/business workflow rather than a foreign key in this Procurement schema.

sections.title: Suggested 12-minute architecture video narrative
items: Minute 0–2: What happens when stable supplies run low? Explain that enterprise buying is a controlled process, not simply clicking “Purchase”.
Minute 2–4: Walk across the ERD: suppliers, requisitions, PO headers/lines and receipt headers/lines.
Minute 4–6: Demonstrate the second-person approval and why authorization is separate from the requester.
Minute 6–8: Receive 60 units, accept 55; show how quantity and stock location connect Purchasing to Inventory.
Minute 8–10: Explain GRNI, the distinction between receipt and supplier invoice, and why AP performs matching.
Minute 10–12: Recap SQL safeguards versus business rules, cross-service calls and audit evidence.
